summary: Gives the architectural description and concept of operations for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: ILNP separates the name of a node from the network location used to reach it. A node can change its Locator while keeping the Identifier used by an active transport session.

questions: how does ilnp separate identity from location
why does splitting ip addresses enable mobility without special protocols
what are the benefits of ilnp multihoming over today's approach
how does ilnp work with existing ipv6 routers
subtitle: An experimental architecture that gives node identity and network location separate roles.

tldr.problem: An IP address identifies a node and also helps locate it in the network. This ties transport sessions to a node's current network location.
tldr.mechanism: ILNP assigns a node an Identifier and a topological Locator. Transport protocols use the Identifier for session state; routers use the Locator to forward packets.
tldr.outcome: The architecture describes mobility and multihoming using changing Locator values while keeping Identifiers stable during a transport session. It is an Experimental Protocol.

facts.label: Locator updates
facts.value: Notify active correspondent nodes of changes

today: RFC 6740 is an Experimental Protocol document from the IRTF. The RFC says its ideas are published for examination, experimental implementation, and evaluation.

sections.title: The Identifier and Locator Split
sections.content:
ILNP is an experimental enhancement to IP described by the IRTF Routing Research Group. It replaces the overloaded role of an IP address with two distinct values: an Identifier names a node, and a Locator names an IP subnetwork.

Transport protocols use Identifiers in session state. The network layer uses Locators for routing and forwarding. This change is intended to let connectivity change without making the node's identity change with it.
sections.plainLanguage: An Identifier names a node, and a Locator names the network where it can be reached. They replace the two jobs that an IP address performs in the existing architecture.

sections.title: Names at Each Network Layer
sections.content:
At the application layer, ILNP recommends names such as a fully qualified domain name. At the transport layer, protocols such as TCP and UDP use the node Identifier. At the network layer, routers use the Locator, which has the meaning of a routing prefix.

An Identifier names the node rather than one of its interfaces. A Locator can change when the node's network connection changes. The pair is called an Identifier-Locator Vector, but it is not equivalent to a single IP address because its two parts have different meanings.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can use a domain name, transport protocols use the node's Identifier, and routers use its Locator. The Identifier names the node; the Locator identifies a network.

sections.title: Transport State and Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
In an IP transport session, the local and remote IP addresses are part of the transport state. In ILNP, the transport state uses the local and remote Identifiers instead. The Locator values are carried for network-layer routing but are not used in the transport-layer session state.

A packet has source and destination Identifier-Locator pairs. Routers forward it using the Locator, while the end systems use the Identifier to associate the packet with the transport session. This lets a Locator change without changing that session's Identifier values.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport state keeps the Identifiers, not the Locators. Routers use the Locators to deliver packets, so a network-location change need not change the transport session.

sections.title: Multihoming and Multiple Paths
sections.content:
A node can bind one Identifier to multiple Locator values. It can then use different network attachments while retaining the same Identifier for a transport session. A transport protocol may use multiple Locator paths, but path selection and management belong to that transport protocol.

For site multihoming, the RFC describes use of provider-assigned Locator prefixes rather than requiring a site to advertise provider-independent prefixes. This is intended to support session resilience without making each site prefix visible in inter-domain routing.
sections.plainLanguage: A node can keep one Identifier and have several Locators for different network connections. A transport protocol can then use more than one path without changing the node's Identifier.

sections.title: Mobility and Locator Updates
sections.content:
ILNP handles mobility by changing a node's Locator values. When a Locator changes, the node sends Locator Update messages to its active correspondents so they can maintain existing network-layer sessions. A host that expects new incoming sessions also updates its Locator records in DNS.

The RFC describes immediate and soft handover. With immediate handover, a host switches to the new Locator. With soft handover, it uses both old and new Locators for a period while connectivity overlaps.
sections.plainLanguage: When a node moves, it can tell active correspondents which Locator changed. It can also update DNS so new connections can find its current Locator.
